Fail Fast, Fail Often, Limited opportunities to fail
I've always been told that someone who doesn't fear failure would fail, then just get back up and try again. And one of the biggest sayings in Silicon Valley is to "fail fast and fail often." That makes sense in the context of R&D, product development, and startups. 

What about when there are limited opportunities to fail? Time and money are very valuable resources. In both scenarios below, assume that you worked really hard, but didn't achieve the desired outcome.

**Time:** Suppose you want to take a certification exam which is only offered once a year. Now if you don't pass the certification exam, then you'll have to wait another year to try again. There's lots of pressure to pass or do well the first time so that you don't waste another year for another attempt. And it feels even worse if you find out you were just a few points away from passing. And those few points costed you another year. In such cases, you don't simply get back up and try again, you'll have to wait another year to try again. 

**Money:** Suppose whatever you are trying to achieve is very expensive for a single attempt, like a major experiment. There's also lots of pressure to get it right the first time around because it's very expensive for a second attempt. Failing could cost you lots of money or even your job. Having another attempt could cost a fortune and take lots of time to set up. This is another case where you don't simply get up and try again. 

In these cases, it's not so easy to just get back up and try again after failing because your next attempt could be a whole year away OR could cost a fortune. I feel that these fears get worse over time because you might have competing responsibilities as you get older. Are such fears valid? If so, how to overcome them?
